content: 1. Greenhalgh et al. reported that 5% of wheelchair users found their device difficult to use. This was based on a quasi-experimental study focusing on secondary complications associated with wheelchair use. 2. Hoenig et al. evaluated wheelchair services provided by rehabilitation experts, which included structured assessments, individually fitted wheelchairs, and additional orders for occupational/physical therapy, equipment, or home modifications as needed. Despite these interventions, there was no significant difference compared to usual care in preventing worsening shoulder pain among older and physically disabled individuals. 3. Greenhalgh et al. also explored inclusion, participation, and quality of life among wheelchair users. They found that 5% of participants completely disagreed that wheelchairs made life complicated, while 3% agreed, and 2% completely agreed that wheelchairs helped bring people together. Additionally, 25% of women in the study completely disagreed with the notion that technology creates isolation. 4. Greer, Brasure, and Wilt (2012) conducted a mixed-methods study on wheelchair abandonment. They concluded that involving individuals in the prescription process may reduce the risk of device abandonment. However, the study had a low MMAT appraisal score of 5/17. 5. Hoenig et al. assessed empowerment and self-esteem among wheelchair users. They found that services provided by rehabilitation experts, including structured assessments, wheelchair training, and follow-ups, did not differ significantly from usual care in improving wheelchair confidence among older and physically disabled individuals. 6. Hansen, Tresse, and Gunnarsson (2004) conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Sweden involving 141 individuals aged over 16 years who used manual wheelchairs. They compared standard interventions with active interventions, which included a one-hour occupational therapy session. The study found that most wheelchairs developed defects over time, and suitability to the user was a critical factor in preventing the device from becoming inappropriate. 7. Leochico and Valera (2020) conducted a case series study in the Philippines involving two patients. Patient A, a 28-year-old female, had partially resolved sacral pressure ulcers but struggled with transferring to and from her wheelchair due to improper technique. Tele-rehabilitation sessions included demonstrations of transfer techniques, practical home exercises, and environmental modifications to improve mobility. Patient B, a 28-year-old male, demonstrated effective pressure-relief techniques and had no new deficits, remaining functional at home and in the community. 8. Di Marco et al. (2003) conducted a mixed-methods study on mobility, posture, and function. They emphasized the importance of systematic follow-ups at 3 and 12 months post-wheelchair issuance. These follow-ups allowed users to identify and address problems early, improving the fit between the user and the wheelchair. This was particularly beneficial for first-time wheelchair users, whose improving strength and skills often required adjustments to their devices. 9. Hansen, Tresse, and Gunnarsson (2004) also studied disruptions in wheelchair use, including breakdowns. They found that 99% of inspected wheelchairs in the active intervention group required attention, with most defects being simple and easily fixable. The study highlighted the importance of regular check-ups to reduce accidents and ensure wheelchair safety and functionality. 10. Leochico and Valera (2020) demonstrated the feasibility of tele-rehabilitation using low-cost technology in resource-limited settings. They emphasized the need for rehabilitation providers to tailor tele-rehabilitation to the technical capacities of healthcare staff and patients while adhering to ethical principles of telemedicine. 11. Di Marco et al. (2003) also explored satisfaction with wheelchair services. They found that systematic follow-ups significantly impacted service delivery by improving the fit between the user and the wheelchair. Telephone reviews provided opportunities to assess user comfort and satisfaction, while face-to-face reviews allowed therapists to evaluate sitting posture and wheelchair durability. 12. Surprisingly, user satisfaction measured with a visual analog scale (VAS) did not increase more in the active intervention group compared to the standard intervention group. This could be due to high baseline satisfaction levels, which left little room for improvement, or the insensitivity of the study design. 13. The findings suggest that active, structured check-ups and systematic follow-ups are critical in addressing secondary complications, improving user satisfaction, and ensuring the long-term functionality of wheelchairs. Further research is needed to determine optimal intervals for check-ups and to explore the potential of tele-rehabilitation in diverse settings.
